visits.text: Road from Essaouira to Agadir along the Atlantic coast: argan trees appear shortly after Essaouira - it's one of the rare places in the world where these trees grow, and goats climbing their branches to eat the fruit are an authentic spectacle (not staged, unlike certain tourist spots). The argan forest is a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

The Kasbah of Agadir Oufella, perched on a hill 236 m above the bay, is the only vestige from before the 1960 earthquake that destroyed the city in 15 seconds. The view from the summit sweeps the entire Bay of Agadir, its 9 km beach, and the Souss mountains behind. The drive or walk up is worth the trip.

Souss Massa National Park, created in 1991 between Agadir and Tiznit, extends across 33,800 hectares of coastal cliffs, dunes, wetlands, and steppes. The Oued Massa estuary is a Ramsar site of international importance for migratory birds: on the 5 km walking circuit, you'll observe flamingos, spoonbills, gray herons, cormorants, and - if you're lucky - the northern bald ibis, one of the world's most threatened species with 95% of the wild population nesting here. Binoculars recommended.

The town of Tiznit, 90 km south of Agadir, is known for its medina ringed by 7 km of pink ramparts and for its silversmiths - the town is Morocco's main center of Berber jewelry. Place du Méchouar and its blue spring are the quiet heart of the old town.

activities.text: Stroll through Souk El Had: 6,000 shops on several levels, spices, textiles, leather, fruit and vegetables. It is a local market, not a tourist market - prices are displayed and there is less pressure than in Marrakech.

4x4 circuit in the park's animal reserves (Rokein and Arrouis): addax with long horns, dorcas gazelles, scimitar oryx, and red-necked ostrich - species extinct in the wild in Morocco and reintroduced here since the 1990s. Visits are mandatory with a park guide.

visits.text: You will cross Tizi n'Tinififft Pass, at an elevation of 1,660 m, on the road from Ouarzazate to Agdz. From the viewpoint, you can see the arid Saghro Mountains, almost devoid of vegetation. The road then descends toward the first palm groves of the Drâa Valley, which begins at Agdz. Stop at the pass for 15 minutes to take in the contrast between the dry rock and the green ribbon of the palm grove.

The Caïd Ali Kasbah overlooks Agdz from a rocky promontory. This 19th-century fortified residence, built of unfired earth bricks, belonged to the caïd, the local governor. Inside, a maze of rooms leads up to the terraces. The building is largely abandoned and belongs to the caïd's descendants: speak with them on-site to arrange a visit.

“Meeting place” is the meaning of Tamnougalt in Tachelhit, the Amazigh (Berber) language of southern Morocco. This ksar, 6 km from Agdz on the other side of the Drâa, was the capital of the Mezguita, the tribe that dominated this part of the valley. Its caïds lived in the Kasbah of the Caïds: three levels of rammed earth surrounding a courtyard, with painted wooden ceilings and carved plasterwork. Some rooms are fragile, so ask before entering. Hire a guide to explore the covered lanes and the former Jewish quarter.

activities.text: In the shade of the date palms in the Agdz palm grove, water flows through seguias, small open-air irrigation channels. They distribute water among plots of henna, mint, and fig trees. Paths connect the douars, the hamlets scattered throughout the palm grove. Set out in the morning with a local guide: they will show you how water flows from one garden to the next and may be able to arrange tea in a local home.

If you are in Agdz on a Thursday, set aside 1 hour for the souk, the weekly market where people from neighboring villages come to sell goods and stock up. Spices, dates, and olives fill the stalls, while the butchers occupy a separate area. This is no tourist market, but part of everyday life in the valley. Come in the morning, before the intense heat.

visits.text: Ochre earthen houses stacked up to the top of a hill: the ksar of Aït-Ben-Haddou looks like a movie set, and it has often served as one. This fortified earthen village, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, appears in Lawrence of Arabia, Gladiator, and the series Game of Thrones. Only a few families still live here. Most residents have settled on the other side of the Ounila River, which runs alongside the ksar: cross it using the pedestrian bridge completed in 2011.

If you still have energy after exploring the narrow streets, climb to the agadir crowning the hill of Aït-Ben-Haddou. This former fortified granary protected the entire village's harvests; only its walls remain. From the summit, the view stretches across the Ounila Valley and the ksar's terrace rooftops. Wear sturdy shoes, as the earthen steps are uneven, and head down before nightfall to return to Ouarzazate, about 30 kilometers away.

visits.text: Al Hoceima is a young city: the Spanish founded it in the 1920s under the name Villa Sanjurjo. A Catholic church from the colonial era still stands in the center. Spanish remains widely spoken here. In the evening, head to Mohammed VI Square. Its ground-level fountains light up at nightfall.

Walk down to Quemado Beach, a few minutes from central Al Hoceima. This is the city beach, just 300 m long. In summer, pedal boats are available for rent, and the beach fills up very quickly. In the off-season, you are more likely to see fishermen bringing in their catch. Come early in the morning to enjoy it while it is quiet.

The best time to stroll around Al Hoceima’s port is late in the day. The Moroccan tourist office recommends walking here to watch the fishermen at work. It is the Rif’s second port after Nador. Ferries also connect it to Motril, Spain. Watch out for ropes and crates: this is a working port, not a marina.

The sand at Sfiha Beach is black, and three islets dot the horizon. One of them, Peñón de Alhucemas, has a fortress and remains under Spanish sovereignty. The 2 km beach belongs to the municipality of Ajdir, the birthplace of Abdelkrim el-Khattabi. This leader from the Rif fought the Spanish army and proclaimed the Republic of the Rif in 1921. In summer, the official count records up to 10,000 swimmers a day: come early.

If Quemado is packed, head to Cala Bonita, another of the city’s beaches. This cove is tucked into a bay enclosed by rocky cliffs. Access is down a few steps, making it less convenient with a stroller. Bring water and a beach umbrella, and arrive early to choose your spot.

activities.text: After 6 p.m., buy your fish directly from the boats docked at Al Hoceima’s port. Then have it grilled at the Club nautique restaurant, the best-known restaurant in the port. Its upper floor overlooks the entire port, making it an ideal place to end the trip in peace. Ask how much grilling costs before ordering.

The coastline of Al Hoceima National Park is best seen from the sea. Small boats leave the port to cruise along the coast. The park is home to a large concentration of ospreys, large birds of prey that dive to catch fish. Negotiate the price and duration before boarding, and bring a windbreaker.

visits.text: Anemiter is worth stopping for: its ksar, a fortified village with earthen walls, is one of the best preserved in Morocco. It lies about 15 kilometers from Télouet, at the start of the Ounila Valley. The painter Jacques Majorelle stayed here in 1921. Park at the top of the village and walk down into the old ksar: the track leading to it is in poor condition.

Though half in ruins, Tamdaght’s kasbah served as the setting for a major scene in director Ridley Scott’s film Gladiator. From Anemiter, plan a round-trip drive through the Ounila Valley to reach Tamdaght. A kasbah is the fortified residence of a prominent family. This one belonged to the Glaoui family, as did the palace in Télouet. Some rooms are no longer accessible. There is no ticket booth or opening hours: knock on the door to ask to enter.

activities.text: You will then head down the Ounila Valley on the P1506, a paved road suitable for a regular car. For about 40 kilometers, the Ounila River traces a ribbon of green farmland between ocher canyons. This valley was a route for caravans carrying salt and goods from the Sahara. Look out for cave dwellings carved into the rock, which served as shelters during conflicts. Without stops, the most scenic stretch takes 1 hour 30 minutes to drive.

visits.text: House upon house, Aroumd rises on a large moraine spur—a mass of rocks and earth left behind by an ancient glacier. At about 1,900 m, it is the highest village in the Aït Mizane Valley, around forty minutes on foot from Imlil. Below, terraces irrigated for a very long time produce barley, corn, and vegetables. The narrow lanes all look alike, making it easy to get lost, so follow the main path or ask for directions.

activities.text: If your legs are up to it, climb from Aroumd to the shrine of Sidi Chamharouch, at 2,350 m, on the Toubkal trail. Allow about two hours for the ascent, with a steep first half, and three to four hours round-trip from Aroumd. You will know you have arrived when you see tea stalls beside the stream, near a small waterfall. The shrine is a pilgrimage site closed to non-Muslims: view it from a distance. A licensed guide is mandatory for this hike on the Toubkal trail.

visits.text: Few Moroccan medinas are as peaceful as Asilah’s. A medina is a fortified old town, and this one is entirely pedestrian. Its ramparts were built by the Portuguese, who captured the city on August 24, 1471. Enter through Bab al-Homer, the Land Gate, and leave through Bab al-Bahr, the Sea Gate. Right beside it, Borj al-Bahr, a bastion completed in 1516, projects into the ocean.

Borj al-Kamra, the main tower in Asilah’s ramparts, rises above Sidi Ali ben Hamdouch Square. It dates to 1509. The Portuguese called it Torre de Menagem, meaning the keep: the strongest tower, where people retreated during an attack. Walk around this massive square structure, then use the square as a meeting point that is easy to find in the medina.

The walls of Asilah’s medina are white, but their appearance changes every year. Since 1978, the Asilah International Cultural Moussem, a festival founded by painter Mohamed Melehi and mayor Mohamed Benaïssa, has had new murals painted on houses each year. The festival includes a summer session and a fall session, with concerts and exhibitions depending on the program. Wander without a route in mind, camera in hand: every alley may reveal a recent mural.

A former bandit had this palace built beside the ocean. Raissouni Palace dates to 1909 and is named after Moulay Ahmed er-Raissouni, the tribal chief who had kidnapped Ion Perdicaris five years earlier. Its reception room combines zellige (a mosaic of small glazed tiles), stucco (carved plasterwork), and painted wood. A terrace overlooks the ocean. Now a cultural center, it opens for exhibitions and events during the Cultural Moussem: at other times, view its facade from the ramparts.

Tombs covered in colorful ceramics descend toward the ocean in Asilah’s seaside cemetery. Walk discreetly along the edge of this Muslim cemetery, without walking between the graves. The overlook above it offers an unobstructed view of the setting sun, with the Atlantic as a backdrop. Arrive half an hour before sunset to find a good spot.

activities.text: If Asilah’s main beach feels too urban, drive south to Rmilat Beach, nicknamed Paradise Beach. This 5 km stretch of sand is wilder than the town beach. The official beach information sheet lists no drinking water supply, so bring water and a beach umbrella.

visits.text: Ochre ramparts overlook a slow-moving river: Azemmour’s medina lines the left bank of the Oum Er-Rbia. The Portuguese occupied it from 1513 to 1541. Estevanico, a native of the city who had been enslaved, left in 1527 with a Spanish expedition to North America. He was one of four survivors out of several hundred men. Today, many walls display murals, portraits, and calligraphy by Moroccan and foreign artists. Wander without a set route, camera in hand.

activities.text: The Oum Er-Rbia estuary begins just a few minutes from Azemmour’s medina. Wetlands, dunes, and green riverbanks attract migratory birds, and a few fishermen still practice traditional fishing here. Come late in the day to photograph the river, then get back on the road: El Jadida is only about twenty minutes away.

visits.text: Carved shells frame the arch of Bab Agnaou, cut from ocher-colored sandstone. Completed around 1190 under the Almohad caliph Yacoub al-Mansour, this gate was the main entrance to the royal kasbah, the sultan’s citadel. Above the arch runs a frieze in Kufic script, an angular form of Arabic calligraphy, featuring verses from the Quran. The meaning of its Berber name remains debated. Stop on the outside to read the frieze, then pass through the gate: the Saadian Tombs are a five-minute walk away.

visits.text: It looks very old, but Bab Bou Jeloud, the grand western gate of the medina of Fez, dates from 1913. The French administration built it as a ceremonial entrance. Its ceramic tiles are blue on the outside and green on the inside. Through the arch, you can already see the minaret of Bou Inania, the religious school you will visit next. Unlicensed guides often wait here. If you want a guide, hire an official one: they must show you their Ministry of Tourism ID. Agree in advance on the price, the route, and a “no shops” rule.

visits.text: Borj Nord kept watch over the enemies of Fez, as well as the city’s own inhabitants. Sultan Ahmed al-Mansour of the Saadian dynasty had this fort built in 1582 on a hill north of the medina. At the time, the people of Fez el-Bali were considered unruly, and the fort was also intended to keep them in check. Today, the fort houses an arms museum: cannons occupy two rooms, alongside sabers, daggers, and rifles. Look for the large firing platform, pierced with 56 openings for cannons. The museum is closed on Mondays.

visits.text: There is nothing to tour, but this is a significant stop: Bouârfa, a small mining town at 1,174 m on the eastern high plateaus, is the first Moroccan bivouac of the 2027 Dakar. It grew around a manganese mine, now closed. Stop here to sleep, refuel and gaze out over the seemingly endless steppe.

activities.text: From January 11 to 14, 2027, the Dakar sets up its bivouac in Bouârfa: stages 2 and 3 loop around the town, and stage 4, covering 750 km, sets off from here toward Zagora. A bivouac is the camp where drivers and mechanics sleep. If you come during the rally, check public access with the organizer.

visits.text: In 1904, the kidnapping of an American in this forest brought the United States Navy to Tangier. Perdicaris Park bears his name: Ion Perdicaris had a villa here, where tribal chief Raissouni kidnapped him on May 18, 1904. President Roosevelt sent seven warships to Tangier, and the hostage was released for a ransom. Since 2022, the restored villa has housed a heritage interpretation center. Afterward, take a walk through Rmilat Forest, overlooking the Strait of Gibraltar.

Cape Spartel marks the point where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Mediterranean Sea, 14 km west of Tangier. Its lighthouse was built in 1864 at the request of European consuls concerned about the many shipwrecks offshore. In 1865, ten foreign countries and Morocco signed an agreement to maintain it jointly. On a clear day, look across the water for Cape Trafalgar on the Spanish coast, 44 km away.

An opening onto the ocean traces the outline of Africa: this is the sight visitors come to see at the Caves of Hercules. Waves carved out these caves, and local people later enlarged them by cutting out millstones for oil presses. According to legend, Hercules rested here before going to pick the golden apples in the Garden of the Hesperides. The ground is dark and slippery: wear sturdy shoes, and come early or in the late afternoon to avoid the crowds.

visits.text: Rabat is not on the road from Agadir: the city is about 87 km from Casablanca, 1 hour's drive north, and is visited as a round trip from Casablanca. The Hassan Tower, an unfinished 12th-century minaret, was meant to be the minaret of the largest mosque in the world according to the Almohad sultan Yacoub al-Mansour. His death in 1199 halted the work at 44 m - half the planned height. The 200 columns of the never-completed mosque now form a silent field of stone around the tower.

The Mausoleum of Mohammed V, facing the Hassan Tower, houses the tombs of King Mohammed V, architect of Morocco's independence, his son Hassan II, and Prince Moulay Abdallah. Built between 1961 and 1971 by 400 Moroccan artisans, its green-tiled pyramidal roof, white Italian marble, and zelliges make it a masterpiece of contemporary Moroccan art. Entry is free and open to non-Muslims.

The Kasbah des Oudayas, a 12th-century Almohad fortress on the Bouregreg estuary, dominates the river and Atlantic. Its blue and white alleys resemble a miniature Chefchaouen. Café Maure, inside the kasbah, is the place for mint tea facing the estuary.

The Hassan II Mosque, built over the sea between 1987 and 1993, is one of the largest mosques in the world, with its 210 m minaret. Its prayer hall can hold 25,000 worshippers, with a further 80,000 people on its esplanade.

Casablanca's downtown Art Deco quarter, built during the French protectorate (1920s-1950s), concentrates one of the world's most remarkable Art Deco architecture collections outside Miami. Place Mohammed V, with its fountains and arcades, is the center. Walk among facades ornamented with geometric forms and Moroccan motifs reinterpreted in concrete.

activities.text: The Chellah, 2 km from central Rabat, combines Roman vestiges of the ancient city of Sala Colonia (1st century) and a 14th-century Marinid necropolis in a garden invaded by storks nesting on the minarets. A historic monument since 1920 and UNESCO heritage since 2012, it's one of Morocco's most unusual sites.
Guided tour inside the Hassan II Mosque for non-Muslims: official providers offer organised tours in the morning and afternoon. Book ahead, places are limited.

Seafood lunch on the Corniche of Casablanca before departure: the waterfront, stretching from the port to Ain Diab, is lined with fish restaurants with terraces on the Atlantic. A final image of Morocco facing the ocean.

visits.text: Blue on the walls, blue on the steps, blue even on the flowerpots: the medina of Chefchaouen is painted from top to bottom, at the foot of the Rif Mountains. It is small enough to explore without a map, letting the sloping streets guide you. Save it for the morning of your second day, before leaving for Akchour. Always ask before photographing someone. The prettiest streets fill up quickly, so get out before the groups arrive.

Return to Outa el Hammam Square in daylight to visit the kasbah, the red-walled fortress that occupies an entire side of the square. Built in the 15th century, it houses a garden and a small museum. Climb its tower for the best view of the rooftops and the mountain. Admission costs around 60 dirhams. The nearby Grand Mosque, recognizable by its eight-sided minaret, is closed to non-Muslims, so you can view it from the square.

Ras el Maa is the spring that supplies Chefchaouen, just beyond the medina’s northeastern gate. Mountain water emerges here in a small cascade, and local women still come to wash clothes. The spot is modest, but it shows everyday life in the city, away from the streets favored for photos. It is also the starting point for the trail to the Spanish Mosque. Allow 20 minutes, longer if you sit by the water.

activities.text: You will arrive in Chefchaouen at the end of the day. Leave the car outside the medina and walk uphill to Outa el Hammam Square, the paved heart of the old town. Its terraces are a good place for dinner after the long ferry day. Save the sightseeing for tomorrow; you are staying here for two nights.

The best souvenir from Chefchaouen folds into a suitcase: the city is known for its textiles, especially the striped blankets worn by women of the Rif. Workshops and stores are found around Outa el Hammam Square and in the nearby streets. Watch a weaver at work before you buy: they will be happy to show you the loom. Compare two or three shops; prices are negotiable. A blanket folds up tightly and fits in a bag.

If you take just one walk in Chefchaouen, climb to the Spanish Mosque late in the day. Built by the Spanish in the 1920s, it was never used. The trail starts at Ras el Maa and climbs for half an hour. From the top, the entire blue city stands out against the mountain, and the esplanade fills up at sunset. Bring a warm layer, then head back down before it gets completely dark.

You will leave Chefchaouen for Akchour, a hamlet in Talassemtane National Park, about a 50-minute drive through the Rif. From the parking lot, a trail climbs for about 45 minutes to the Bridge of God, a natural rock arch spanning the Farda River far below. You can walk across the arch itself to reach the opposite slope. Leave early: the site gets very busy in good weather. Wear proper hiking shoes.

visits.text: More than 20,000 whitewashed graves cover Miâara Jewish Cemetery, the largest in Morocco. Near the entrance, some graves are painted blue. These belong to the Cohanim, descendants of the priests of the Temple in Jerusalem. Men, women, and children are buried in separate sections. One corner of the cemetery holds around 6,000 children who died during a typhus epidemic in the 19th century. Men are lent a kippah at the entrance, and a donation to the caretaker is customary. Avoid Saturdays and Jewish holidays.

visits.text: In 1910, Thami El Glaoui, the future pasha of Marrakech, meaning the city’s governor, commissioned Dar El Bacha. He wanted it to be luxurious enough to impress his guests. Since 2017, the palace has housed the Museum of Confluences, dedicated to Moroccan decorative arts and objects from other cultures. Its exhibitions change regularly. Damaged by the 2023 earthquake, the museum reopened as early as November of that year. It is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 AM to 6 PM and closed on Mondays. Expect to pay around 60 dirhams.

activities.text: Extend your visit at Bacha Coffee, the café set in a historic salon at Dar El Bacha. This café specializes in arabica, a variety of coffee bean. Reservations are not accepted, and a line may form at busy times. Coffee is charged separately, in addition to museum admission.

visits.text: In El Jadida, walk along the citadel that houses the Portuguese Cistern: its interior is closed for restoration and cannot be visited. This chamber, approximately 34 m on each side and supported by 25 pillars, may have served as an arsenal before becoming a water reservoir in 1541. Before the closure, a thin layer of water covered the floor and reflected the vaults. A shaft of light fell through a round opening that once collected rainwater. Orson Welles filmed a scene here for his Othello, released in 1952. Stay outside the construction site.

Next, you will climb a steep ramp onto the ramparts of Mazagan, the former Portuguese name for El Jadida. About 8 m high and 10 m thick, they have a 2 m-wide wall walk. The star-shaped fortress dates from 1541–1548, and UNESCO listed it in 2004. The Portuguese left in 1769: the empty city was nicknamed “the ruined one,” then renamed El Jadida, “the new one,” in the 19th century. From the Bastion of the Angel, the view stretches over the ocean and harbor.

The Sea Gate, at the end of the Portuguese city’s main street, is the old passage where ships unloaded their goods. Beneath a nearby arch, a communal oven still bakes bread brought by women from the neighborhood. Near the entrance, the Church of the Assumption is built in the Manueline style, the Portuguese Gothic style of the early 16th century. The Grand Mosque, right next door, has a five-sided minaret. Ask before photographing local residents at the oven.

visits.text: El Jebha means “the forehead” in Arabic: the Rif Mountains frame this small port like a forehead above the sea. Under the Spanish protectorate, the town was called Puerto Capaz. Its port shelters many fishing boats and also welcomes recreational boaters cruising along the coast. Walk around the docks before getting back on the road.

activities.text: If you pass through on a Tuesday, stop at El Jebha’s souk, one of the largest and liveliest in the region according to the Moon guide. A souk is a traditional market. On other days, head down to the 1.8 km sand-and-pebble beach at the mouth of the Ouringa, a small river. There are no showers or restrooms: bring water.

visits.text: Erg Chigaga is Morocco’s largest erg, a sea of sand dunes. It stretches for around 40 kilometers between Jbel Bani to the north and the hamada, a stony plateau, toward M’Hamid. Some dunes rise more than 50 m high. Until around 1990, this was a military zone, and few travelers came here. Even today, there are no roads or villages, only camps. Bring a warm jacket, as nights are cold even after a scorching day.

activities.text: Climb a large dune in Erg Chigaga an hour before sunset. Take your time: in soft sand, every step takes much more effort than it would on a trail. From the summit, the dunes’ shadows stretch eastward, and the silence is almost complete. Keep a headlamp handy for the descent, and locate the camp lights before night falls.

Slow, swaying, and a little hard on the back, a dromedary camel ride is still the most fitting way to experience Erg Chigaga. You can even reach the erg from M’Hamid on a multiday trek with a caravan. For a first experience, a one-hour ride from camp is enough. Request it when booking your desert camp stay, and wear long pants for greater comfort in the saddle.

With no villages for tens of kilometers around, Erg Chigaga’s night sky is dark enough to photograph the stars. The organized desert camp, a tent camp set up by a tour operator, provides dinner and sleeping accommodations. Before booking, ask how the camp manages water and waste: in such a dry environment, it matters. If possible, choose a date near the new moon, when the sky is darkest.

If you get up half an hour before dawn, you will see Erg Chigaga’s dunes turn from gray to pink, then gold. The morning sand is still cool and holds the tracks left overnight by small desert animals. Walk for an hour before breakfast, then pack your bag for the return trip by 4x4 to M’Hamid, where your car awaits.

visits.text: Beginning in 1760, French engineer Théodore Cornut designed part of Essaouira’s medina for Sultan Sidi Mohammed ben Abdallah. The city combines European-style ramparts with Arab-Muslim architecture, earning it UNESCO World Heritage status in 2001. Its port, oriented toward sub-Saharan Africa, long earned it the nickname “Port of Timbuktu.” In late June, the Gnaoua Festival fills the city. Dedicated to Gnaoua music, a Moroccan musical tradition, it also welcomes jazz and reggae: book your accommodations early.

Climb onto the Skala de la Kasbah, the cannon-lined rampart on the medina’s northwestern side: a row of old cannons still points toward the ocean. The platform, accessible at any hour, is a meeting place for the city’s young people. Essaouira’s ramparts served as a filming location for season 3 of Game of Thrones, depicting the fictional city of Astapor. Visit before sunset if you want to enter Bab Ljhad, the northern bastion, which closes at that time.

Blue boats packed along the docks and fishermen mending their nets: Essaouira’s fishing port is first and foremost a working harbor. Carpenters still build wooden boats here, sold throughout Morocco and as far away as France. Sardines and conger eels make up most of the catch. In the market hall at the port entrance, watch the fish auction. Go in the morning, then continue to the Skala du Port, right next door.

There are no signs or audio guides: the Skala du Port, an 18th-century fortified battery, is worth visiting for its cannons and views. From the Borj el-Barmil corner tower, you can see the port and the Mogador Islands, about 1.5 km offshore. These islands form a nature reserve where Eleonora’s falcons, birds of prey, come to breed. In antiquity, King Juba II had purple dye produced here from shellfish. Expect to pay around 60 dirhams; open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. The wind is often stronger in the afternoon.

Bayt Dakira, the “House of Memory,” tells the story of Jewish life in Essaouira, a city where Muslims, Jews, and Christians have lived side by side since its founding. It is in the former mellah, the Jewish quarter. Inside are the restored Simon Attias Synagogue, Torah scrolls, silver Hanukkah lamps (for the Jewish Festival of Lights), marriage contracts, and photographs from the 19th and 20th centuries. King Mohammed VI visited in January 2020. Admission is free; closed Saturdays. Clothing that provides coverage is recommended.

activities.text: More interesting than the souvenir stalls, the woodworking shops built into the space beneath the Skala de la Kasbah let you see Essaouira’s artisans at work. They carve thuya, a local conifer whose root wood is used. This craft has been practiced in the medina for centuries. You can watch the wood progress from a rough stump to a finished object.

When the wind blows, as it often does, Essaouira Bay fills with kitesurfing kites. The city is nicknamed the “City of Trade Winds,” after the steady winds that sweep this coast. Partly sheltered by the Mogador Islands, the bay is suitable for beginners: several schools offer kitesurfing, windsurfing, surfing, and stand-up paddleboarding. For your first session, choose a school that provides supervision from the beach and has a rescue boat.

visits.text: Bab Boujloud, nicknamed the Blue Gate, is the most convenient entrance to Fez el-Bali, the old city of Fez. Beyond its arch, two streets lined with shops descend toward the heart of the medina: Talaa Kebira, the “large ascent,” and Talaa Sghira, the “small” one. Remember the name of the gate: everyone knows it, making it a useful landmark when you need to find a taxi.

Carved cedarwood, intricately worked plaster, and glazed tiles from floor to ceiling: the Bou Inania Madrasa is a former Quranic school near Bab Boujloud. It was built by the Marinids, the dynasty that ruled Morocco in the late Middle Ages. Its ablution room with running water is a rarity. The courtyard takes 20 minutes to visit. Come when it opens, around 9 a.m., before the groups arrive.

Founded in 1325 to house students from the neighboring mosque, the Al-Attarine Madrasa is smaller than Bou Inania and just as decorated. It takes its name from the spice souk surrounding it. The Qaraouiyine Mosque, right next door, is closed to non-Muslims: you can only glimpse its courtyard through the doors. Visit both madrasas in the morning to compare them.

If you are concerned about the smell, accept the sprig of mint offered at the entrance: Chouara Tannery, the largest in Fez, has a strong odor. Hides are treated in round vats filled with dyes of every color. You can watch from above, on the terraces of the leather shops surrounding the courtyard. Bags and slippers will be offered to you on the way down; you are under no obligation to buy.

The Nejjarine Fondouk was a caravanserai, an inn for merchants: animals and goods occupied the ground floor, while travelers stayed upstairs. Restored, it now houses the Museum of Wood Arts and Crafts. Inside, you can see objects made by Fez artisans. In front of the entrance, the tile-covered fountain in Nejjarine Square is worth a photo. Allow 40 minutes for the whole visit.

You can hear the hammering before you arrive: in Seffarine Square, coppersmiths, artisans who work with copper and brass, still hammer their wares into shape in the open air. The square is very close to the Qaraouiyine Mosque, in the heart of Fez el-Bali. Sit down for a mint tea and watch them work. If something catches your eye, compare prices at two or three shops before bargaining.

If the narrow streets feel overwhelming, leave the medina and walk to Jnan Sbil Garden, Fez’s large public park. You will find shade under tall trees, palm-lined paths, and a pond reflecting the branches. The garden is generally open every day, but check the hours locally. Allow a good half hour, with time to sit down before returning to the souks.

Fez Jdid, “New Fez,” is the city’s second historic district, founded by the Marinids next to the old medina. It is home to the Royal Palace, which can only be viewed from the outside, and the nearby former Jewish quarter. The area is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List along with Fez el-Bali. Allow 45 minutes for the walk; there are no monuments to visit inside, so it is a chance to soak up the atmosphere. Save it for late in the day, when the heat eases.

activities.text: The best dinner in Fez is eaten standing up in Rcif Square, at the bottom of the medina. At dusk, the square fills with street vendors. Try harira, a tomato, lentil, and chickpea soup, and msemen, flaky flatbreads. Choose the stalls where families are lining up.

You will leave the car outside the walls: Fez el-Bali, the old city of Fez, can only be explored on foot, through a maze of narrow streets. Founded between 789 and 808, it has been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1981. For a first visit, hire an official guide: they will lead you from one monument to another through the souks and help you avoid the fake guides stationed at the gates. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for walking, in addition to the time spent at each site. Agree on the price and duration before setting off.

visits.text: Foum Zguid means “the mouth of the Zguid wadi”; a wadi is a desert watercourse. This small oasis town in Tata Province marks the transition from the Anti-Atlas to the Sahara. Walk in the shade of its palm grove, then visit the remains of the old kasbah on the outskirts. On Thursday mornings, the weekly souk brings the main street to life.

activities.text: You can watch carpet weavers, leatherworkers, and jewelers at work at Foum Zguid’s craft center, which opened in 2022. The town is also the closest to Iriqui National Park, established in 1994 to protect desert wildlife. Its lake, usually dry, filled within a few days after heavy rains in October 2024. No paved road leads there: access is via a dirt track and requires a 4x4 with a driver.

visits.text: Gdourt, in the Aït Mansour Gorges, is known for its tightly clustered rammed earth houses clinging to the mountainside above the palm grove. In fall, the palms bear dates; in January–February, the almond trees bloom. Greet residents before photographing them, and stay on the paths, as the gardens are cultivated.

activities.text: At the bottom of an arid red-rock canyon, the Aït Mansour Gorges shelter a palm grove that stays green year-round. Allow two hours to walk along the stream, among date palms, almond trees, and olive trees watered by seguias. In 2018, the FAO, the United Nations food agency, recognized the argan-based agriculture of Aït Souab and Aït Mansour as a globally important agricultural heritage system. The road is paved as far as the entrance to the valley; beyond that, the dirt road may require a 4x4.

visits.text: A vertical rock face, carved into strange shapes, borders the river at the bottom of the Oued Laou gorges. The valley is part of Talassemtane National Park, established in 2004. Since 2006, the park has also been part of a UNESCO biosphere reserve, a protected area spanning Morocco and Spain. Barbary macaques, tailless monkeys classified as endangered, frequent these cliffs. Keep your distance and never feed them.

activities.text: Head up the valley on the P4105, a paved road with little traffic, stopping on the shoulders to look at the river. The Moroccan firs that are the park’s reason for being grow much higher up, at elevations between 1,400 and 2,000 m. Here, you are exploring the lower part of the park, shaped by water. The park covers nearly 60,000 hectares, almost six times the area of Paris. Turn back whenever you like to spend the night in Oued Laou.

visits.text: At 6.5 km from the entrance to Dadès Gorge, the Aït Youl kasbah looks like a Moroccan travel poster: a pink earthen house set in front of almond and fig trees. It belonged to the Glaoui, the pasha who held power in the south. Stop by the roadside. A child from the village will offer to guide you for around twenty dirhams.

The winding road at Tisdrine is the most famous image of Dadès Gorge: a series of hairpin turns climbing the cliff. It takes a few minutes to drive up. The viewpoint is at the top, past the last turn. Drive slowly and keep right.

activities.text: Locals call them the “monkey fingers”: at Tamlalt, in the Dadès Valley, the cliff is made of fused pebbles that form large, rounded fingers. You can see them from the road. To get closer, take a guided walk through a narrow canyon. Wear closed-toe shoes and skip the walk in rainy weather.

visits.text: The temperature drops and voices echo as you enter Todra Gorge, near Tinghir. Along the final 600 m, two smooth cliffs 160 m high face each other just ten or so meters apart. The road runs along the bottom beside the river. Come early for a peaceful walk.

activities.text: Next, walk through the Tinghir palm grove, a strip of gardens that follows the river to the entrance of Todra Gorge. Paths wind between cultivated plots, irrigation channels, and old earthen villages. Just under an hour is enough for a change of scenery. Stay on the paths to avoid damaging the crops.

visits.text: At an elevation of about 1,700 m, Igherm is an Anti-Atlas crossroads where the roads from Taroudant, Taliouine, and Tafraoute meet. An agadir, a fortified communal granary, survives on the edge of town, although rebuilding has altered its form. Stop for tea in the center before taking the narrow road down to Tafraoute.

visits.text: In Amazigh, the Berber language, Imi n’Ifri means “the mouth of the cave.” This natural bridge, 6 km east of Demnate, is what remains of an enormous cave, most of which has collapsed. Many birds nest in its vaulted ceiling. A trail with about 300 steps leads down to the bottom of the gorge and passes beneath the arch. This section is exposed and has no railing: you need to be sure-footed and comfortable with heights.

Demnate, a small town at the foot of the High Atlas, retains its old ramparts and its kasbah in the center. A large Jewish community lived here from the early 12th century until the late 1950s. It was known for its wine and leatherworking. Olive groves surround the town. If you visit on a Sunday, stop by the weekly souk, where you can find red clay pottery.

visits.text: The most beautiful part of Imlil is not its main street, lined with outdoor gear shops, but the terraced orchards surrounding it. At an elevation of 1,740 m, the village is the usual starting point for climbing Toubkal, North Africa’s highest peak at 4,167 m. The September 2023 earthquake hit the valley hard, and reconstruction continues. Toward the end of the day, follow the small irrigation channels that water the terraces: they reveal how these slopes are farmed.

activities.text: Walk uphill from Imlil to the village of Tamatert, at 1,810 m, along a path lined with walnut, apple, and cherry trees. In the surrounding villages, each family tends a few walnut trees. Their walnuts have shells so hard that they are soaked in water for 1 or 2 days so they can be cracked cleanly. If you still have energy, continue to Tizi n’Tamatert Pass, at 2,272 m. Head back down before nightfall: the trails are not lit.

visits.text: More than 500 m on a single wave: that’s possible in Imsouane Bay when the swell comes from the right direction. This fishing village has a point break, a wave that consistently forms in the same place and peels along a rocky headland. The bay’s slow, steady wave suits beginners and longboards. The faster wave at La Cathédrale is for experienced surfers only. The bay works best from low to mid tide.

activities.text: Imsouane’s small harbor still relies on fishing: the village boats supply the fresh fish sold on-site. It’s a good stop on the road between Essaouira and Taghazout to watch the surfers and stretch your legs. Allow about 1 hour 15 minutes for the onward drive to Taghazout.

places.name: Majorelle Garden

visits.text: To enjoy Majorelle Garden before the crowds, book the first time slot at 8 AM: the site receives more than 700,000 visitors a year. Painter Jacques Majorelle began creating this garden in 1923 and opened it to the public in 1947. He gave his name to Majorelle blue, the intense cobalt blue that covers his villa. Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé bought and restored the property in the 1980s. The fashion designer’s ashes were scattered here in 2008. Tickets are sold exclusively online through the garden’s official website.

The Pierre Bergé Museum of Berber Arts occupies Jacques Majorelle’s former painting studio in the heart of the garden. Opened in 2011, it introduces the Amazigh, the name the Berbers use for themselves, a people who have lived in North Africa for millennia. Its galleries span the Rif to the Sahara, displaying jewelry, clothing, weapons, carved doors, rugs, and musical instruments. One section also explores Berber Jews. Museum admission is separate from garden admission: add it when booking. Open from 8:30 AM to 5 PM.

visits.text: Do not come to the Menara Gardens expecting flower beds: this is a vast olive grove surrounding a pool, with a single, beautiful view. The pavilion with its green tile roof, completed in 1870, is reflected in the water, with the Atlas Mountains in the background on clear days. The pool, built in the 12th century, is elevated, allowing water to flow down to the olive trees by gravity. The water comes from the Atlas Mountains through khettaras, underground tunnels. Admission to the garden is free; the pavilion costs 60 dirhams.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

activities.text: Catch your breath in Jnan Sbil Garden, created in the 19th century by Sultan Moulay Hassan I. It lies between Fez el-Bali, “Old Fez,” and Fez el-Jdid, “New Fez,” built in the 13th century by the Marinids. Its 7.5 hectares, roughly the equivalent of ten soccer fields, were restored from 2006 to 2010 and reopened in 2011. You will find a large pool, a bamboo garden, and norias, the large wheels that draw water for irrigation. Al Batha Museum is then a 10-minute walk away.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: A broad expanse of water among dry hills, with the High Atlas peaks as a backdrop on clear days: this is Lake Lalla Takerkoust. It is an artificial reservoir. Its dam was built between 1929 and 1935, during the French protectorate, on the Oued N’Fis (oued means river). The water irrigates the Haouz Plain around Marrakech and is also used to generate electricity. Come before 9 a.m. or in the late afternoon, when the lake is calmer and the light on the mountains is softer.

If you have binoculars, follow the western shore of Lake Lalla Takerkoust, the best side for birdwatching. A narrow paved road runs for about 5 km along this shore, with several viewpoints along the way. During the spring and fall migrations, you may spot ruddy shelducks, reddish ducks; black-winged stilts, with their very long legs; or ospreys, birds of prey that dive for fish. Their numbers depend on the water level. A spotting scope makes observing them much easier.

activities.text: Swimming is officially prohibited in Lake Lalla Takerkoust, but you can still head out onto the water. Rental operators along the shore offer pedal boats, small motorboats, and Jet Skis. Some also advertise swimming areas: check the rules on-site before entering the water. The lake is calmer on weekdays. In summer, avoid midday, when the heat is intense and shade is scarce.

visits.text: White facades and café terraces: Liberation Square is the lively heart of Larache. The Spanish occupied the city twice, from 1610 to 1689 and then from 1911 to 1956. During the protectorate, they named this square Plaza de España. Its Arab-Andalusian style recalls nearby Andalusia. Have a coffee at an outdoor table and watch the city go about its day.

Pass through Bab el-Medina, the gate opening onto the square, to enter Larache’s medina. Souk Esseghir, the small market, leads to narrow streets that descend to the fishing port. Then return to the central market, 200 m from the square, a renovated covered building in the Andalusian style. Go during the day, when the stalls are at their liveliest.

If you could take away just one view of Larache, it would be the one from Balcon Atlantique. This viewpoint, whose name means “balcony over the Atlantic,” overlooks the ocean. Travel guides rank it among the city’s finest views. Come at the end of the day to watch the sun set over the sea, then walk back to the center.

French writer Jean Genet is buried in Larache’s old Spanish cemetery, at the end of the waterfront promenade. He had lived here for several years and asked to be buried here; he died in 1986. Spanish writer Juan Goytisolo, who died in 2017, is buried in the same cemetery. Be discreet: this is a place for quiet reflection, with no visitor facilities.

activities.text: End the day at Larache’s fishing port, below the medina. The fish landed here help give the city its reputation, along with the region’s oranges and berries. Choose a simple local eatery and ask for the day’s fish, grilled. Confirm the price by weight before it is cooked.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima

visits.text: In 2000, the grounds of Le Jardin Secret were just a pile of rubble divided among more than 130 owners. Yet in the 19th century, one of the medina’s largest riads—houses built around an interior garden—stood here. Caid U-Bihi, a powerful local leader, had it built. Restored with private funding, the site opened to the public in 2016. English landscape designer Tom Stuart-Smith created two gardens here: an Islamic garden with geometric paths lined with citrus trees, and an exotic garden arranged around a large jacaranda tree. Admission is 100 dirhams, free for children under 12.

activities.text: Climb to the top of the tower at Le Jardin Secret for a view over the medina’s rooftops. On your way down, follow the channels and pools in the Islamic garden. They were supplied by khettaras, underground tunnels dug to bring groundwater into the city. These old channels have been restored. The tower ticket costs 40 dirhams in addition to admission. Children under 6 are not allowed in the tower.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: On the hill of Lixus, 80 m above the Loukkos River, the Phoenicians built a city in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE. These seafarers came from present-day Lebanon. Follow the path to the temple district, the largest excavated area of the site. The city’s economy depended on salted fish, shipped in amphorae—large earthenware jars whose fragments can still be found. The site is open daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., and admission costs 80 dirhams for a foreign adult.

Pliny the Elder, a Roman scholar of the 1st century, placed the Garden of the Hesperides, guarded by a dragon, at Lixus. To him, this dragon was simply a metaphor for the Loukkos River, which snakes across the plain in broad loops. Start at the interpretation center, opened in 2019, where panels help make sense of the rather inconspicuous ruins. Then head uphill to look at the river’s meanders: you will see Pliny’s dragon.

visits.text: There are no palaces or gardens here, but faces: the Maison de la Photographie showcases photographs of Morocco dating back to the 1870s. Two collectors, Parisian Patrick Menac’h and Marrakech native Hamid Mergani, assembled these vintage prints. Portraits fill the ground floor. Near the rooftop, a documentary about the High Atlas, filmed by Daniel Chicault in 1956, is screened. Finish on the terrace with a juice or coffee overlooking the rooftops. Open from 9:30 AM to 7 PM; admission is 50 dirhams.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: The Koutoubia is Marrakech’s main mosque, 200 meters from Jemaa el-Fna Square. Its pink sandstone minaret, built in the 12th century, stands about 77 m tall and is visible from many parts of the city. Its name comes from the booksellers who once worked at its base. Non-Muslims are not permitted inside. Walk around to the gardens behind the building for the best view and some peace and quiet.

Allow a good hour for Bahia Palace, a ten-minute walk south of Jemaa el-Fna Square. The palace has a succession of large courtyards and rooms decorated in intricate detail from floor to ceiling. The walls and ceilings are the main attraction. Admission costs 100 dirhams for foreign visitors in 2026. Come when it opens, as the narrow corridors fill up quickly.

If you arrive when the Saadian Tombs open, around 9 a.m., you’ll have them almost to yourself. This 16th-century royal cemetery holds the graves of the Saadian dynasty, beneath cedar ceilings and among marble columns. Walled off for two centuries, it was rediscovered in 1917. The site is small and the line grows quickly. Combine your visit with El Badi Palace, a few minutes away on foot.

A ruin, but an impressive one: El Badi Palace was built in the 16th century by the Saadian sultan Ahmed al-Mansour. Only high earthen walls and an immense courtyard remain. Storks nest on top of the walls. One room displays the Koutoubia’s minbar, the wooden pulpit from which sermons were delivered. Come in the late afternoon, as there is little shade in the courtyard.

Founded in the 14th century and rebuilt in the 16th, Ben Youssef Madrasa was a Quranic school that could house up to 900 students. They lived in 130 small cells arranged around a central courtyard. Covered in tilework, carved plaster, and cedar wood, the courtyard appears in countless photographs of Morocco. Admission costs 50 dirhams. Go upstairs to see the cells, then come back down when the courtyard empties out.

Electric blue walls, green plants, and the sound of water: Majorelle Garden is a peaceful retreat outside the medina of Marrakech. Fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent fell in love with it. The paths are narrow and visitors are plentiful. Book your ticket online several days in advance, especially during school vacations, and choose the opening time slot at 8 a.m. A petit taxi can take you there from the medina.

Step inside Le Jardin Secret, in the Mouassine neighborhood, when Marrakech’s souks have worn you out. This restored 19th-century palace contains two gardens: one with exotic plants, the other laid out in the Islamic tradition. Sit in the shade and enjoy the quiet. There is an admission fee. Save it for early afternoon, when the medina is at its most stifling.

activities.text: Smoke from the grills, drums, and vendors calling out: Jemaa el-Fna Square changes character at dusk. Food stalls set up in the center, surrounded by musicians and performers. Five times a day, the call to prayer from the Koutoubia rings out over the crowd. Always ask prices before sitting down or taking a photo. For a break, head up to the terrace of a café on the edge of the square.

On January 23, 2027, the Dakar ends in Marrakech with a final loop around the city and the final podium ceremony. The day before, stage 11 arrives there from Smara after more than 1,000 km. If you’re in town on those days, expect large crowds. The organizer determines the podium location and public access: check the official schedule before heading out.

Spend a morning getting lost in the souks of Marrakech, the network of covered lanes north of Jemaa el-Fna Square. Trades are grouped by street: leather, copper, textiles, and spices. The first price quoted is only a starting point, so feel free to negotiate and remain friendly. If you’re not buying, a simple “no thank you” is enough. If you’re unsure of the way, ask a shopkeeper rather than a passerby offering to guide you.

There is nothing more relaxing to end your stay than a tour of Marrakech’s ramparts in a calèche, a horse-drawn carriage. The long wall surrounding the medina passes by at a walking pace, with its gates appearing one after another. It’s the best way to appreciate the size of the old city. Agree on a price before setting off, for a specific route and duration. Ask your accommodation where to find a carriage and what price to aim for. Choose late afternoon, when the heat eases.

visits.text: Drive from Ouarzazate to Marrakech via the Tichka pass (2,260 m): it is the highest pass on Morocco's national road. The climb is long and the hairpins are many - the landscapes change radically with each altitude. At the top, stop for the view over both sides of the Atlas. Allow 3.5 to 4 hours of driving.

Arrival in Marrakech mid-afternoon. First approach to the medina's ochre ramparts, 19 km long and dating from the 12th century - they give the city that characteristic tint earning it the nickname 'red city'. Settle into a medina riad for total immersion.

The Koutoubia Mosque, built in the 12th century by the Almohads, is one of North Africa's largest mosques with its 70 m minaret - the model for Seville's Giralda. Not accessible to non-Muslims, but the surrounding gardens offer an unobstructed view of the entire tower. Morning recommended for light.

The Bahia Palace, built in the late 19th century by Grand Vizier Si Moussa, extends across 8 hectares of gardens, interior courtyards, and decorated apartments. Its name means 'the brilliant' - the painted cedar ceilings, mosaics, and moucharabiehs justify the appellation. Visit is self-guided, allow 1 hour.

The Saadian Tombs, rediscovered in 1917 beneath a layer of plaster, house the sepulchers of 66 members of the Saadian dynasty including Sultan Ahmad al-Mansour (died 1603). The main hall, decorated with 12 Carrara marble columns, is a jewel of Hispano-Moorish art. Arrive at opening (9am) to avoid the line.

The Majorelle Garden, created from 1923 by a French painter and purchased in 1980 by a couturier who saved it from destruction, is Morocco's most visited garden. The intense cobalt blue of the structures - christened 'Majorelle blue' - contrasts with the green of bamboos and cacti. Book online: capacity is limited and queues without reservation are long from 10am. Arrival at opening recommended.

The fashion and art museum adjacent to Jardin Majorelle traces the history of a great French couture house through its archives, sketches, and a selection of iconic pieces. The building's architecture in ribbed red brick is itself remarkable.

Marrakech's Mellah, historic Jewish quarter adjacent to the royal palace, preserves ancient synagogues and distinctive architecture with its overhanging balconies. The Lazama Synagogue, from the 16th century, is the most accessible and best preserved.

activities.text: First evening on Jemaa el-Fna square: at nightfall, the square transforms into a permanent spectacle - storytellers, snake charmers, Gnawa musicians, orange juice stands, and smells of grilled skewers. It's been UNESCO-listed as intangible cultural heritage since 2001. Arrive at 7pm to watch the square gradually come alive.

Dive into Marrakech's souks: each street has its specialty - leather, spices, babouches, brass, carpets. The dyers' souk (Souk des Teinturiers) is most spectacular, with wool skeins hanging from facades in red, yellow, and violet. Bargaining obligatory and advised with a smile.

Traditional hammam in late afternoon: medina hammams offer the complete package - steam, scrubbing with kessa glove, black beldi soap, and argan oil massage. Allow 1.5 hours. A way to close two days of walking through the souks.

activities.text: In summer, Martil Beach receives up to 80,000 people a day, according to the official beach survey. This seaside resort is the closest to Tetouan, northeast of the city. Its sand stretches for 4 km to the mouth of the Martil River, which the Spanish called Río Martín. Walk along the waterfront, then rejoin the coastal road heading southeast.

visits.text: Small but exquisite, the Al-Attarine Madrasa may be the day’s loveliest surprise. Allow 30 minutes to visit. Its name comes from the adjacent Al-Attarine souk, the spice and perfume market. The Marinid sultan Abu Said Uthman had it built from 1323 to 1325. Look at the bronze-clad cedar entrance doors: they are copies, since the originals are preserved at the Al Batha Museum. Upstairs are around thirty student rooms. Admission is 20 dirhams, payable in cash.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Ben Youssef Madrasa, a former Quranic school that housed students, is the largest in Morocco. The Saadian sultan Abdallah al-Ghalib completed it in 1564–1565. Its 130 rooms surround a courtyard where a shallow pool reflects the carved facades. The school could accommodate up to 800 students. Head upstairs to see how cramped the rooms are, with light coming in from the courtyard. Closed in 2018 for restoration, the madrasa reopened in April 2022. It is open daily from 9 AM to 7 PM; admission is 50 dirhams.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: From floor to ceiling, no wall is bare in the Bou Inania Madrasa, a religious school that housed its students. At the bottom is zellige, a mosaic of small, colorful ceramic tiles; above it is carved plaster; higher still is carved cedar. Sultan Abu Inan of the Marinid dynasty had it built from 1350 to 1355. It is the only madrasa in Morocco that also served as a congregational mosque for Friday prayer. Its prayer hall, reserved for Muslims, can be seen from the courtyard. Admission is 20 dirhams; it closes during prayers, with a longer closure on Fridays.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Road from Chefchaouen to Meknes with a stop at Volubilis, Morocco's largest Roman site: 42 hectares of UNESCO-listed ruins, founded in the 3rd century BCE. At its peak, the city had between 10,000 and 20,000 inhabitants. The Arch of Caracalla (early 3rd century CE), the Villa of Venus mosaics, and the forum are the centerpieces. Go before 10am - after that, the heat is punishing and there's no shade on site.

3 km from Volubilis, the holy village of Moulay Idriss Zerhoun clings to two hills shaped like camel humps. This is the resting place of Idris I, founder of Morocco's first Muslim dynasty and the country's first Islamic king. Every summer, for more than a month, the village hosts the Moussem (pilgrimage) of Moulay Idriss, one of the most important in Morocco.

Meknes, nicknamed the city of the 'Moroccan Louis XIV': Sultan Moulay Ismail made it his capital from 1672 and endowed it with 40 km of ramparts pierced by 20 monumental gates. Bab Mansour, main gate to the imperial city, is one of Morocco's most imposing. The Mausoleum of Moulay Ismail, open to non-Muslims, is a masterpiece of zellige and stucco.

activities.text: Evening stroll through Meknes' medina: less touristy than Fes or Marrakech, it has retained an authentic character with its butchers, grocers, and artisans working in their shops.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Morocco: From Tangier to the Sahara Dunes

visits.text: In the mid-15th century, the Jews of Fez settled beside the Royal Palace in the Mellah neighborhood. The word means “salty place,” perhaps because of a saltwater spring or a former salt warehouse. On Rue Bou Khessissat, opened in 1924, Jewish houses have balconies facing the street. The Ibn Danan Synagogue, dating from the late 17th century, reopened in 1999 after restoration. From its roof, you can see the white tombs of the Jewish cemetery. Admission prices vary: ask on arrival.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: The Mellah, Marrakech’s former Jewish quarter, begins at Place des Ferblantiers. Artisans still make metal lanterns by hand in this square. The neighborhood emerged in the mid-16th century, next to the royal kasbah. It had around 40,000 residents in the late 1940s. Today, around 200 Jews remain in Marrakech. In the narrow streets east of the main street, look for the small Stars of David on doors and grilles. The neighborhood is free to explore: ask before photographing residents.

activities.text: Shop for spices at the Mellah’s covered market, where stalls display ground spices in tall pyramids. The secret behind these perfect cones is a metal mold hidden inside. Look for ras el-hanout, a spice blend whose recipe varies from shop to shop. It often contains white pepper, ginger, turmeric, and cumin. Cumin is the main spice grown around Marrakech: choose round seeds, a sign of quality.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: Erg Chebbi is a sea of dunes on a stony plateau just outside Merzouga. An erg is a field of dunes formed by the wind. The highest reach around 150 m, as tall as a fifty-story building. On this first evening, simply watch the sand change color at sunset.

It is sometimes called the “Black Village”: Khamlia, 7 km from Merzouga, is home to Gnawa people, descendants of enslaved people from sub-Saharan Africa. Their repetitive, almost hypnotic music was once used in healing and blessing rituals. A village association welcomes visitors for a short concert over tea. Leave a banknote or buy a record before you go: that is how the musicians earn their living.

activities.text: You’ll leave Merzouga by camel in the late afternoon to reach a camp in Erg Chebbi. The camels walk at a steady pace as the sand turns orange. Hold firmly onto the handle when your camel stands up and lies down. The camps also offer transfers by 4x4. Cover your head and mouth with a chèche, a long scarf: the wind kicks up sand.

Silence falls suddenly when the engines stop: a night at a camp in Erg Chebbi is spent in a tent among the Merzouga dunes. Dinner is followed by music around the fire. Far from any city, the sky is filled with stars. From October to May, nights are cool: bring a fleece and a hat, even if the day has been warm. Camps range from basic tents to tents with bathrooms.

If you’re willing to get up before dawn, climb the dune closest to camp to watch the sun rise beyond Erg Chebbi, toward Algeria. Climb along the ridge, where the sand is firmer, and allow twenty to thirty minutes for the ascent. At the top, dunes stretch as far as the eye can see. You can run back down in a few minutes. Shake out your shoes before leaving.

Less poetic than a camel ride, but much more efficient for seeing the area: a 4x4 tour around Erg Chebbi takes you around the Merzouga dunes in one to two hours, depending on the stops. You’ll cross the stony plateau surrounding the sand, then pass through villages at the foot of the dunes, including Khamlia. Ask the driver to stop at a high point so you can appreciate the size of the erg. Agree on the price and number of stops before getting in, and avoid the midday hours.

visits.text: “M’Hamid of the gazelles”: the name M’Hamid El Ghizlane recalls the gazelles that once lived on the nearby plains. The last oasis along the Drâa before the desert, it was long a stop for caravans crossing the Sahara. Several ksour, fortified earthen villages, lie hidden in its palm grove, including M’Hamid Bali and Ouled Driss. Most are almost empty and crumbling. Ask before entering a house: some require a small contribution.

The modest ruins of Ksebt El Allouj in M’Hamid are worth visiting mainly for the history they evoke. They are generally dated to the Saadian dynasty, which ruled Morocco in the late 16th century, when the oasis depended on trade across the Sahara. No one knows exactly what the building was used for. Make it the destination of a short walk through the palm grove, with a local resident as your guide.

activities.text: You will leave your rental car in M’Hamid El Ghizlane, where the N9 ends. The 50 to 60 km leading to Erg Chigaga consist entirely of unpaved tracks across stony plateaus, ancient dry lake beds, and soft sand where vehicles easily get stuck. Book a 4x4 with a driver and an overnight stay at an organized desert camp, a tent camp run by a tour operator, in advance. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours for the journey.

The sand begins right at the edge of M’Hamid El Ghizlane: small dunes are within walking distance or a short dromedary camel ride away. At sunset, their crests turn orange as the palm grove falls into shadow. It is a good warm-up before Erg Chigaga. Set out an hour before sunset and return before it is completely dark.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: The religious and scholarly heart of Fez since the 9th century, Al Quaraouiyine Mosque stands at the center of the medina. According to tradition, Fatima al-Fihri, the daughter of a wealthy merchant from Kairouan, Tunisia, founded it around 857 or 859. Al Quaraouiyine University grew around this mosque. Guinness World Records describes it as the oldest educational institution still operating in the world. The mosque is closed to non-Muslims. Through an open doorway, you can glimpse part of the courtyard: stay on the threshold and avoid prayer times.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: “The booksellers’ mosque”: that is what Koutoubia means, a name recalling the booksellers’ souk that once surrounded it. Its 77 m minaret, completed in the late 12th century, serves as a landmark in the medina. Each of its four faces has a different arrangement of decorative arches: walk around it to compare them. On the esplanade, you can see the foundations of an earlier mosque. It is believed to have been replaced around 1158 because it was incorrectly aligned toward Mecca. The mosque is closed to non-Muslims: you can view the exterior free of charge.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: Al Batha Museum of Islamic Arts occupies Dar Batha Palace, the sultans’ summer residence in the late 19th century. Converted into a museum in 1915, it reopened on February 26, 2025, after six years of restoration. Among its roughly 700 works, look for the minbar from the Mosque of the Andalusians, a carved wooden pulpit more than a thousand years old from which the imam preaches. The Andalusian garden, designed in 1915, is divided into four sections around a fountain. Admission is 60 dirhams, with opening hours from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., except Tuesdays; allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: As early as 1711, traveling merchants slept upstairs at the Nejjarine fondouk and stored their goods on the ground floor. A fondouk was a merchants’ inn built around a courtyard. Since 1998, the building has housed the Nejjarine Museum of Wooden Arts and Crafts. Inside, you will see carved doors, musical instruments, and wooden tablets made by students at the Quranic school. In the courtyard, the large scale was used to weigh goods. The museum is open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Finish at the rooftop café, with views over the medina’s roof terraces.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Seen from the street, the facade of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum resembles fabric: its terracotta bricks form a woven pattern. Designed by the French firm Studio KO, the building opened in October 2017, just steps from Majorelle Garden. The permanent gallery displays around fifty haute couture pieces. They are rotated regularly to preserve them. The museum is open from 10 AM to 6 PM and closed on Wednesdays. Book a combined ticket with the garden on the official website.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: The water is as still as a lake and the air smells of salt along the Nador corniche, the palm-lined promenade beside the Marchica lagoon. This 115 km² lagoon is separated from the Mediterranean by a belt of dunes. Walk along it late in the day, when the city comes out for some fresh air.

activities.text: On January 11, 2027, Dakar competitors disembark in Nador after an overnight crossing, then travel by road to Bouârfa without being timed. No race stage takes place here: this is the rally’s entry point into Morocco. The port is in Beni Ensar, around 15 km from the center. Ferries arrive here from Almería year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: Around the Dakar 2027: From the Algarve to Marrakech in 22 Days

visits.text: Calm water on one side, Atlantic breakers on the other: Oualidia’s lagoon is protected from the ocean by a sandbar. At low tide, the water recedes and sandy islets emerge. The beach along the lagoon offers sheltered swimming areas, and Moroccan families come here for their summer vacations. Stay on the lagoon side: facing the ocean, the shore break—the first waves near the shore—is dangerous even in mild weather.

Oualidia takes its name from Sultan El Oualid of the Saadian dynasty, who had a kasbah built in 1634 to defend the entrance to the lagoon. Along the waterfront, a palace built around 1940 for the future King Mohammed V now stands abandoned. It still belongs to the royal family, however. You can view its arcaded galleries from the beach. Take this short walking loop in the late afternoon, after your swim.

activities.text: “Oysters taste best when eaten right in the water,” says an Oualidia guide quoted in the Moroccan press. Oyster farming was introduced here in 1956. Pacific oysters are raised in beds recognizable by their wooden stakes. Beach shacks serve the oysters raw, with lemon. They are also the town’s main export.

If you visit between fall and spring, Oualidia’s lagoon fills with birds arriving to spend the winter or stopping along their migration routes. It is part of the Sidi Moussa-Oualidia Ramsar site, a wetland protected by an international convention since 2005, where 114 species of waterbirds have been recorded. Small boats follow the shores, where you can see gray herons, spoonbills, egrets, and flamingos stopping between Spain and Senegal.

You can also explore Oualidia’s lagoon at your own pace in a kayak or on a stand-up paddleboard rented on the beach. Sheltered by the sandbar, the water stays calm, which is reassuring for beginners. On the ocean side, a beach shack also rents surfboards. Go in the morning, when the beach is quieter.

days_plan.itin_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout

visits.text: Stop in the Dadès Gorges en route from Merzouga: the pink limestone cliffs close in on the road until forming a vertiginous corridor. At the gorges' entrance, the 'monkey fingers' - rock formations eroded into grotesque bulbs - are one of the strangest landscapes in pre-Saharan Morocco. Allow 30 to 40 minutes.

The ksar of Aït Ben Haddou, 30 km from Ouarzazate, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1987. This fortified village in pisé and raw earth, built from the 17th century on the trade route between Sudan and Marrakech, has served as a backdrop for some twenty Hollywood films - Gladiator, Game of Thrones, Lawrence of Arabia. Climb to the collective granary (agadir) atop the ksar for panorama over the Ounila Valley.

The Kasbah Taourirt, built in the 19th century for the powerful Glaoui tribe, dominates Ouarzazate from downtown. A section is open for visits: stucco-decorated apartments, interior courtyards, and terraces offer a glimpse of Berber luxury of the era. Allow 45 minutes.

Excursion south into the Draa Valley: from Ouarzazate, the valley stretches for 200 km through palm groves, pise villages and kasbahs. The road first crosses the Jbel Saghro by the Tizi n'Tinififft pass, then reaches the valley at Agdez: from there the finest landscapes begin - palm trees, market gardens, and kasbahs appearing at every bend in the road. Allow a full-day round trip from Ouarzazate.

activities.text: Dinner on a terrace in Ouarzazate facing the Atlas: the city, at 1,160 m altitude, marks the frontier between mountains and desert. The Draa Valley palm groves begin here.

Visit the Atlas Studios of Ouarzazate: one of the world's largest open-air filming complexes, used since the 1960s for productions from Lawrence of Arabia to Babel. Guided tours access sets still standing - Jerusalem, Rome, or Egyptian ruins in papier-mâché amid the desert. It's kitschy but fascinating.

visits.text: Five kilometers of sand between the mountain and the sea: welcome to Oued Laou Beach. The town, 44 km from Tetouan, relies mainly on fishing outside the summer season. In summer, vacationers arrive and festivities bring the town to life. Walk along the sand to the river mouth, where the Oued Laou River flows into the sea.

activities.text: The best meal in Oued Laou is a plate of grilled sardines. The Moon guide describes this fishing port as a quiet town where people eat sardines and tagines. Settle into a small restaurant near the port and ask for the catch of the day. On Saturday, browse the souk, the weekly outdoor market.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima

visits.text: Bab Sidi Abdelwahab is the main gateway to the medina of Oujda, built around 1335 under the Marinids, the ruling dynasty at the time. Standing 9 m high, it opens onto a broad esplanade that was long the center of city life. This is the way to enter the old town. Come in the late morning, when the esplanade comes to life.

It won’t take long to explore Oujda’s medina: it is small, and its walls and squares have been restored. The stalls mainly sell food, and the region’s olives are renowned. Try some before sitting down at a café. Allow 45 minutes for the whole visit.

For a break before the long road south, Lalla Aïcha Park is a good choice: it is Oujda’s largest green space, with 17 hectares of palm trees and walking paths. There is nothing to tour, just shade and a café. Stock up on water and supplies here: beyond Oujda, towns become few and far between.

Located 400 m from Bab Sidi Abdelwahab, Lalla Meryem Park is an enclosed garden next to Dar Sebti Palace. It has a small museum and cool paths where locals come to sit. It makes a short stop between the medina and lunch. Check on site whether the museum is open.

days_plan.itin_title: Around the Dakar 2027: From the Algarve to Marrakech in 22 Days

visits.text: The Oumesnat Traditional House is a former family home turned living museum in the Ammeln Valley, about 6 km from Tafraoute. Arranged on several levels around a central kitchen, it shows how local people lived in the 18th and 19th centuries. The owners often lead the tours, which have an admission fee. To get there, leave the main road and follow the dirt road toward Jbel Lekst and the signs for “Maison Traditionnelle.”

Oumesnat’s lanes climb the mountainside between rammed earth houses, some partly carved into the rock. Higher up, the ruins of the old village crumble on the slope. In January–February, almond trees bloom all around. After visiting the Traditional House, climb through the lanes before getting back on the road to Taroudant.

activities.text: Take one of the trails starting in Oumesnat, such as the “Lion’s Head” loop. This name refers to the rocky flank of Jbel Lekst, a 2,359 m peak with the Ammeln Valley stretching out at its foot: seen from a particular spot on the road, it forms the shape of a lion’s head. The trail offers sweeping views of the valley, which has about twenty Berber villages. Bring water and sturdy shoes, as the slopes are steep.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: You hear Ouzoud Falls before you see them: their roar rises from the gorge as soon as you reach the first viewpoints. The water drops about 110 m in several tiers before flowing into the gorge of the Oued el-Abid, the river below. A maintained trail from the village of Tanaghmeilt leads to the foot of the falls in 15 to 20 minutes. There is no official admission ticket. Arrive early in the morning: it gets very crowded in summer.

Ouzoud is thought to come from an Amazigh word meaning “olive,” and olive trees do indeed surround the falls. About ten small traditional olive oil mills still operate along the river. Stop at one on your way down to Ouzoud Falls: it is a chance to see an old-fashioned mill at work, just steps from the water.

activities.text: Climb into one of the small shared boats waiting at the foot of Ouzoud Falls. Local operators steer them across the pool to get as close as possible to the main falls. From below, you get a better sense of the water’s 110 m drop. There is a charge for the ride: agree on the price before boarding, and put your phone in a waterproof pouch.

If you encounter Barbary macaques around Ouzoud Falls, do not feed them. They are a protected species and the only monkeys living in the wild in Morocco. Feeding them disrupts their natural behavior. To watch them, follow the loop trail that crosses the river at the foot of the falls and takes about 1 hour. Keep your bags and food securely closed.

The trail through the Oued el-Abid gorges is worth the effort: it takes you far from the crowds gathered near Ouzoud Falls. The falls plunge into these gorges, and the site is part of the M’Goun UNESCO Global Geopark. A geopark is an area recognized for the richness of its rocks and landscapes. These trails are less traveled than the area around the falls: go with a licensed local guide and plenty of water.
