visits.text: Look up in every room of Bahia Palace, whose name means “the Brilliant”: its painted cedar ceilings are the highlight of the visit. Grand Vizier Si Moussa, the sultan’s prime minister, began construction in the 1860s. His son Ba Ahmed expanded it until 1900, bringing the palace to around 150 rooms. The grand courtyard, measuring 50 m by 30 m, is paved with Carrara marble. Damaged by the 2023 earthquake, the palace is still undergoing restoration. Open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission is 100 dirhams, payable in cash.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: Badi means “the Incomparable,” yet all that remains of this palace are immense earthen walls surrounding pools and gardens. Sultan Ahmed al-Mansour began building it in 1578. He likely financed it with the ransom paid by Portugal, which Morocco defeated that year. The Italian marble used for the columns was traded for its weight in sugar. Around 1707, Sultan Moulay Ismaïl had the palace dismantled to reuse its materials in Meknes. Damaged by the 2023 earthquake, the site reopened as early as October. Admission is 100 dirhams, payable in cash.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: If you arrive early, you will have the gates of the Royal Palace of Fez, known as Dar al-Makhzen, almost to yourself. The palace covers 80 hectares, the equivalent of more than a hundred soccer fields. It is not open to visitors. Its seven gates on Place des Alaouites were built from 1969 to 1971. Their gilded bronze doors are covered in geometric patterns and framed by blue zellige and carved cedar. Photograph the gates, but not the guards, and do not get too close.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Jemaa el-Fna square changes throughout the day. In the morning, orange juice vendors, snake charmers, and artists working with henna, a plant-based dye applied to the skin, set up in the half-empty square. Around 4 p.m., cooks assemble their stalls. At sunset, musicians and Berber troupes draw crowds, often until around 1 a.m. In 2001, UNESCO recognized the square for its storytellers and street performers. For a view of it all from above, head to a café terrace at the edge of the square.

activities.text: Have dinner on the benches at Jemaa el-Fna’s food stalls, which light up as night falls. Try snail soup, skewers, tagine, or fried fish. Choose a busy stall, eat with bread instead of utensils, and drink bottled water. Arrive early in the evening to find a seat. The French Ministry for Foreign Affairs reports bag and phone thefts in Marrakech: keep your valuables close to you.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: The ringing of hammers on copper guides you to Seffarine Square. Its name means “coppersmiths,” the artisans who work copper. Their workshops were documented here as early as the 16th century. Even today, they hammer out large cauldrons here. Seffarine Madrasa, built in 1271, also opens onto the square: it is Morocco’s oldest building originally constructed as a madrasa. It still houses students and is not open to visitors. Settle beneath the old tree to watch the artisans, and ask before photographing a workshop.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Thirteen hairpin turns and a climb of about 750 m over 19 km: the road from Lake Lalla Takerkoust up to the Kik Plateau must be earned. It first crosses dry hills, then winds upward to an elevation of about 1,320 m. Stop at one of the final bends wherever the shoulder allows: the lake comes into view below. This climb is well known among cyclists, so take care on the curves.

Moulay Brahim overlooks the gorges that bear its name, along the road descending from the Kik Plateau toward Asni. This holy village is clustered around the mausoleum of Moulay Brahim and draws many visitors from Marrakech. The shrine is a place of prayer: view it from the lanes without trying to enter. Farther down, Asni holds its weekly souk on Saturdays. If you pass through that day, stop for 1 hour to browse the stalls.

activities.text: Park on the Kik Plateau and walk for 1 to 2 hours among wheat fields and villages. The earthen Berber houses follow the mountain slope and blend into it. On the paths, donkeys and mules remain the surest way to reach the hamlets. In spring, snowmelt brings the meadows into bloom. The villages are very modest: bring water and a picnic, and always ask before photographing anyone.

days_plan.itin_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud

visits.text: Walls painted blue and white line the narrow streets of the Kasbah of the Oudayas, the citadel overlooking the mouth of the Bouregreg River. Enter through Bab Oudaia, a gate carved between 1195 and 1199 for Sultan Yacoub el-Mansour of the Berber Almohad dynasty. In the 17th century, Moriscos, Muslims expelled from Spain, settled here and founded a republic of privateers that attacked merchant ships. Rue Jamaa leads to the semaphore platform, a former station that sent signals to ships. Come early, before the tour groups.

More recent than it looks, the Andalusian Garden of the Oudayas was created between 1915 and 1918. This was the beginning of the Protectorate, the period when France administered Morocco (1912–1956). With its bougainvillea and citrus trees, the garden imitates those of Al-Andalus, medieval Muslim Spain. Nearby Café Maure offers a chance to take a break on the terrace. Save this garden for the middle of the day, between the kasbah and the medina.

Rabat’s medina, the old city surrounded by ramparts, is best explored without a fixed plan. Its Rue des Consuls, laid out in the 17th century, housed major merchants and foreign delegations until 1912. Farther along, Souk as-Sabbat is nicknamed the street of shoes. To the southwest, the Mellah was the neighborhood where Jewish families traditionally lived. Allow 1 hour to wander: the Kasbah of the Oudayas is just a few minutes away on foot.

Though unfinished, Hassan Tower is even more impressive than a completed minaret. Sultan Yacoub el-Mansour began construction in 1196 for an enormous mosque, but work stopped when he died in 1199. The tower reaches 44 m, instead of the planned height of more than 60 m. Inside, ramps replace stairs: the muezzin, the man who calls people to prayer, was meant to be able to ride up on horseback. The rows of columns in front mark the prayer hall, ruined by the earthquake of 1755. From the center, allow 30 minutes for the uphill walk, or take a petit taxi.

If you enjoy ceremonies, watch the royal guards on horseback outside the Mausoleum of Mohammed V: they generally agree to be photographed. Completed in 1971, this white marble monument with a green roof was designed by Vietnamese architect Cong Vo Toan. It houses the tombs of Mohammed V, a hero of independence, his son Hassan II, and Prince Moulay Abdallah. Non-Muslim visitors view the tombs from an interior balcony. Cover your shoulders and knees; the tourist office lists weekday opening hours as 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Chellah brings together two eras across 7 hectares above the Bouregreg River. Below, Sala, an ancient Roman city, preserves the remains of its forum, a temple, and a triumphal arch. Higher up lies the Marinid necropolis, the cemetery of a dynasty that ruled Morocco during the Middle Ages. Enter through a gate completed in 1339. Storks nest on the minaret. Eels live in a pool: according to a local belief, feeding them helped women have children. Following restoration, the site reopened in 2024: 70 dirhams, or 120 with an audio guide.

days_plan.itin_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout

activities.text: Cumin, saffron, and paprika add color to the stalls of Rahba Kedima, a small, sunny square amid the souks. It is also known as Spice Square. Shops around its edges sell spices, traditional cosmetics, and herbal remedies. Some offerings are surprising, such as dried lizards. In the center, women sell woven baskets and cotton caps. Several cafés line the square, making it an ideal place to take a breather away from the narrow passageways.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

places.name: Rissani

visits.text: The birthplace of the dynasty that rules Morocco today, Rissani is home to the mausoleum of Moulay Ali Chérif, the ancestor of the Alaouite kings. The yellow building stands on the southern edge of town. Ask at the entrance which areas are open to non-Muslims. Modest clothing that covers the body is recommended.

Let’s be honest: little remains of Sijilmassa, just two gates and a few earthen walls on the outskirts of Rissani. Founded in the eighth century, the city once controlled the caravans crossing the Sahara. It was destroyed for good in 1818. Ten minutes is enough, for the history more than the view.

activities.text: Stock up at the Rissani souk, the region’s main market, which is busiest on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Sundays. Spices, leather, and livestock are sold here. Try medfouna, a stuffed bread that is a local specialty. Park outside the market and keep some change handy.

visits.text: It is best to visit Safi’s National Ceramics Museum before Potters’ Hill: you will then understand what you are looking at. The museum occupies the Kechla, a fortress listed as a historic monument, and its terrace offers views over the city. Its seven rooms trace Moroccan ceramics from prehistory to the end of the 20th century, from the Rif Mountains to the High Atlas. One room honors Boujemaa Lamali, a master potter associated with the pottery school that opened in Safi around 1920. Open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.; closed Tuesdays.

activities.text: Earthen kilns and their chimneys rise across Safi’s Potters’ Hill, visible from the Bab Chaaba gate at the edge of the medina. This neighborhood, listed as a historic monument since 1920, houses cooperatives where artisans mainly preserve traditional techniques. Safi is renowned for its blue ceramics. Walk among the workshops and watch the potters throw pots—that is, shape clay on a wheel.

days_plan.itin_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout

visits.text: A contemporary art garden in the Ourika Valley may come as a surprise, but Anima Garden makes the combination work. Austrian artist André Heller opened it in 2016, 27 km south of Marrakech. Plan a round-trip drive from Setti Fatma to visit the garden. Across three hectares, ceramic sculptures and pools mingle with plantings, with the Atlas Mountains as a backdrop. Arrive when it opens, at 9 a.m., to enjoy the peace and quiet. Admission is around 140 dirhams per adult: check the price before you go.

activities.text: Setti Fatma’s first waterfall is only the beginning: the seven-waterfall hike takes more effort higher up. The village, deep in a gorge, is the last in the Ourika Valley accessible by paved road. A steep trail leads to the base of the first and largest waterfall in twenty minutes. Another ten minutes of almost vertical climbing brings you to a viewpoint with a refreshment stand. It takes another hour of effort to reach the highest waterfall. Avoid weekends and summer, when residents of Marrakech flock here.

In the Ourika Valley, a village’s name can tell you its market day: Tnine Ourika comes from tnine, meaning “Monday” in Arabic. This is where the valley’s large weekly souk takes place every Monday. Farther up the valley, Aghbalou hosts a smaller market on Thursdays. From Setti Fatma, plan to drive down the valley to reach these markets. If you are visiting on either day, set aside an hour to browse the stalls, preferably in the morning.

visits.text: A golden sand beach stretching as far as the eye can see and a white tomb facing the ocean: Sidi Kaouki takes its name from this marabout, the tomb of a local saint. Every August, a moussem, a festival honoring the saint, brings this small Berber village 25 km south of Essaouira to life. The rest of the year, the atmosphere remains peaceful despite the surf schools. Swim with caution: the ocean here is often rough, with strong currents.

activities.text: In Sidi Kaouki, you will find schools renting boards and wetsuits for beginners and experienced surfers alike. The beach break works almost year-round, with the biggest swells arriving in winter. Suitable for beginners, it works best around high tide. From September to March, conditions are better for surfing. From April to October, the steady wind tends to attract kitesurfers and windsurfers.

visits.text: Founded in the seventeenth century and still in the hands of the same family, the Amridil kasbah is a large fortified earthen house at the entrance to the Skoura palm grove. It appeared on the old 50-dirham bill. Inside, you can see an olive press, bread ovens, and old wooden locks. Climb up to the roof.

activities.text: Continue with a walk through the Skoura palm grove, a patchwork of small irrigated gardens beneath palm, almond, and pomegranate trees. Other earthen kasbahs, in various states of ruin, appear among the trees. The paths all look alike, so use the Amridil kasbah as a landmark to find your way back.

days_plan.itin_title: Around the Dakar 2027: From the Algarve to Marrakech in 22 Days

visits.text: If you visit the dyers’ souk before noon, you will see artisans working over their vats. Skeins, those long loops of wool, dry above the alley in yellow, blue, or red. Natural colors come from saffron, indigo, poppies, or cochineal, a small insect that is crushed. Many workshops now use chemical dyes. Admission is free: turn down anyone claiming that a guide is required. A close-up photo of an artisan often costs 10 to 20 dirhams.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

activities.text: The best part of Marrakech’s souks is wandering without a particular destination. Start at the northeast corner of Jemaa el-Fna and head up to Souk Semmarine, the main covered passageway. Its slatted roof, once made of reeds, is now metal to reduce the risk of fire. Farther along, the passage branches off toward other souks, each originally associated with a trade: leather, metalwork, jewelry, or carpets. Bargain with a smile, but never go back on an agreed price.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: The water is lukewarm and clear at the Blue Spring of Meski, a pool surrounded by palm trees on the edge of the Ziz Valley. Natural springs emerge from the ground here, and the Foreign Legion enlarged the basin to create a swimming pool. There is a small entrance fee. People stop here mainly to stretch their legs.

If you arrive before evening, cross the river downstream from the spring and climb to the ksar of Meski, a fortified village of earth and stone that is now abandoned. The regional tourist office dates it to the 12th century. From the top of the ruins, the Ziz palm grove forms a green ribbon through the stony desert. Wear sturdy shoes.

days_plan.itin_title: Around the Dakar 2027: From the Algarve to Marrakech in 22 Days

visits.text: The Mellah’s loveliest surprise is hidden behind an unmarked door: Lazama Synagogue (Slat al-Azama). According to tradition, it was founded in 1492 by Jews expelled from Spain. A courtyard tiled in blue and white leads to the prayer hall. There, zellij mosaics made from glazed terra-cotta tiles form a Star of David. The rooms around the courtyard tell the story of Jewish life in Morocco. Visit Sunday through Thursday: during Shabbat, access is reserved for worshippers.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: In 1984, Belgian artist Jean Vérame painted blue a group of large granite boulders rounded by erosion, south of Aguerd Oudad, near Tafraoute. The colors have faded over time, and most of the rocks have since been repainted. The blue contrasts with the pink granite and pale sand. Come early in the morning: the low-angle light brings out the colors, and the heat is still bearable.

Pink granite mountains surround Tafraoute, a small Anti-Atlas town at an elevation of about 1,000 m. Its name comes from the Amazigh word tafrawt, meaning “basin” and, by extension, “valley.” In the center, a small market sits on a knoll overlooked by a minaret, amid renovated lanes. The town is liveliest on Wednesday, the main market day.

activities.text: Walk south from Tafraoute toward the village of Aguerd Oudad, overlooked by a granite rock nicknamed Napoleon’s Hat: its silhouette resembles the emperor’s bicorne, a two-pointed hat. The path follows a dry riverbed to the painted rocks. Farther on, vegetation takes over the riverbed: head back up to the small road at that point. Allow a good two hours and wear closed-toe shoes.

Tafraoute bills itself as the capital of the Berber babouche, a round-toed leather slipper that is often brightly colored. Shops in the center sell them alongside amlou, an almond and argan oil spread that is a regional specialty. Taste the amlou on a piece of bread before buying. For babouches, try several sizes and take your time bargaining.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: Locals call the rock at the end of the beach south of Taghazout Imouran, meaning “the dying”; it is also nicknamed Devil’s Rock. According to oral tradition, fighters killed battling the Portuguese in the 16th century are said to have been buried there. This Berber fishing village, 19 km north of Agadir, saw hippies arrive in the late 1960s, followed by surfers. The beach stretches for about 7 km to the rock: set out early if you want to walk its length.

Anchor Point, 3 km north of the village of Taghazout, is a long wave that peels along a rocky headland. With a good swell, it continues as far as the Hash Point surf spot and ends on Panoramas Beach. Conditions are best from September to April. Even if you’re not surfing, settle on the rocks to watch the surfers, keeping out of their way.

activities.text: Take your first surf lesson in Taghazout, where schools and rental shops line the village. To get started, choose a sandy beach over a rocky point like Anchor Point: the bottom is less dangerous if you fall. The region’s waves are best from September to April. Allow half a day for travel, getting equipped, and the lesson.

To find out where argan oil comes from, visit a production workshop around Taghazout: alongside fishing and tourism, it is one of the village’s sources of income. The argan tree grows wild in southwestern Morocco. The know-how associated with it, passed down mainly by women, has been on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2014. The fruit is harvested and dried, the pits are cracked, and the kernels—the seeds inside—are ground before the paste is kneaded with warm water.

days_plan.itin_title: Morocco’s Atlantic Coast in 8 Days, from Rabat to Taghazout

visits.text: Residents call it the “village bank”: the agadir of Aït Kine, a fortified communal granary a ten-minute drive from Tleta Tagmoute, still stores barley, dried fruit, and valuable documents. Archives document its use as early as 1708. Each family has its own room, 76 in total, plus a room reserved for the tribe. A caretaker opens the door at dawn and closes it at sunset: come during the day and ask him for a tour.

activities.text: Park upstream from the Tleta Tagmoute oasis and continue on foot: the seguias, small irrigation canals, guide you from one plot to the next. Pomegranate and olive trees grow beneath the date palms, with grains, vegetables, and alfalfa for livestock in their shade. This layered planting protects the lower crops from the scorching sun. Allow forty-five minutes for the walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

activities.text: “The Great Climb”: that is what Talaa Kebira means, the sloping street linking Bab Bou Jeloud to the heart of the medina of Fez. There are no cars here: the medina is one of the largest urban pedestrian zones in the world. Goods travel on donkeys or handcarts, so give them the right of way. Farther down, look for the mosaic-decorated minaret of the Chrabliyine Mosque. Shops nearby still sell traditional shoes. Take your time wandering and compare prices before buying.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: A pinch is enough to flavor a dish: saffron is the specialty of Taliouine, a mountain town at the foot of Jebel Siroua. At the Maison du Safran and the Souktana cooperative, founded in 1979, you can learn how the flowers are picked at dawn in October and November. Buy it here in threads, never as a powder.

On the way out of Taliouine, you’ll see a large, half-ruined earthen kasbah: the Glaoui Kasbah, named after the former pasha of Marrakech. No sign points it out, so look for it from a distance. Its decorated walls can be viewed from outside; part of it houses a guesthouse.

visits.text: A 13th-century Quran copied onto gazelle skin is the centerpiece of the library at the Naciria Zawiya in Tamegroute. A zawiya is the headquarters of a Sufi brotherhood, part of a mystical tradition within Islam, and also serves as a place of teaching. This one dates back to 1575 and still holds several thousand manuscripts on medicine, mathematics, and astrology. Access depends on the caretaker being present: ask in Zagora before setting out, and put your camera away, as photography is generally prohibited.

activities.text: No two pots are quite the same green: in Tamegroute, the shade of the glaze, a coating that turns glassy during firing, varies with the heat of the kiln. The village potters still fire their pieces in traditional kilns, and local tradition traces this craft back to Fez. Step into a workshop to watch the pottery being thrown, then compare the shades before buying. On Saturdays, the village souk also displays their pottery.

You will see your first dunes a few kilometers south of Tamegroute, at Tinfou. They are much smaller than those of Erg Chigaga, but offer enough sand for a first barefoot walk. Stop for half an hour in the early afternoon, then set off again to reach M’Hamid before nightfall: driving at night is discouraged in Morocco.

visits.text: The kasbah of the Caïds of Tamnougalt, near Agdz, was the residence of the chiefs who governed this part of the Drâa Valley. Its origins are thought to date back to the sixteenth century. A village resident guides you from room to room, up to the rooftops overlooking the palm grove. Agree on the price before the visit.

activities.text: If you have an extra half hour, walk down into the Drâa palm grove at the foot of Tamnougalt. You can walk along canals in the shade of date palms. Djebel Kissane, a long mountain, closes off the horizon to the north. The road then follows the valley, passes through Zagora, and continues 20 km to Tamegroute before you return to Zagora.

days_plan.itin_title: Around the Dakar 2027: From the Algarve to Marrakech in 22 Days

activities.text: Pick up your rental car at Tangier Ibn Battouta Airport, southwest of the city. Tangier deserves a trip of its own: on this itinerary, its airport serves only as the starting point for the Atlantic coast. Before signing the rental agreement, ask how much it costs to drop off the car in Al Hoceima. The route ends nearly 300 km from Tangier, on the Mediterranean.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Morocco in 6 Days: Asilah, Tetouan, and Al Hoceima

activities.text: You will disembark at the port of Tanger Med, your gateway to Morocco on this trip. After passport control, customs will issue the vehicle’s temporary admission document free of charge, authorizing your car to travel in the country. Present the original vehicle registration document. Keep this document until you leave Morocco.

days_plan.itin_title: Around the Dakar 2027: From the Algarve to Marrakech in 22 Days

visits.text: Arrival in Tangier and first immersion in the medina: the Grand Socco, former marketplace, marks the crossroads between the colonial town and the old city. The Kasbah, perched atop the medina, houses the Dar el Makhzen - the former sultan's palace converted into a museum, displaying Roman mosaics and ethnographic collections. Climb to the terrace: the view sweeps across the Strait of Gibraltar and, on clear days, the Spanish coastline.

14 km west of Tangier, Cap Spartel is the extreme northwestern point of continental Africa: this is where the Mediterranean and Atlantic meet before your eyes. The lighthouse dates from 1864 - climb to the platform to watch the two seas merge into one. The sight is more impressive than you'd imagine.

5 km from the cape, the Caves of Hercules open onto the Atlantic through a fissure whose shape eerily resembles the map of Africa. The site has been occupied for over 7,000 years BCE - archaeologists found stone tools here. According to legend, Hercules rested here before completing his eleventh labor. Come early morning to avoid the crowds; entry opens at 9am.

activities.text: Wander the medina's alleys in late afternoon: the souks come alive, the scents of spices mingle with those of warm bread, and shopkeepers close up for the day. This is when Tangier reveals its true character, far from organized tours.

Mint tea at Café Hafa, perched on a cliff overlooking the strait since 1921: generations of writers and artists have set down their notebooks here facing the horizon. Settle on the terrace to watch ferries pass between two continents.
After the caves, walk along Achakkar Beach at the foot of the cliffs: it's a wild, uncrowded beach where you can stroll along the rocks. A good contrast to the bustle of Tangier's port.

visits.text: Climb to the terrace of a leather shop for an overhead view of Chouara Tannery, the largest of Fez’s three tanneries. The hides first soak in white vats containing water, salt, lime, and pigeon droppings: the ammonia in the droppings softens the leather. They then move into the dye vats, with poppy red, indigo blue, or henna orange. Access to the terrace is free, but leave 10 to 20 dirhams if you do not buy anything. If someone tells you “the tannery is closed today,” it is a trick to take you elsewhere.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: Taroudant’s kasbah, the former royal quarter in the northeast of the city, was built in the 17th century by Sultan Moulay Ismaïl. Enter through Bab Sedra, its old gate, to explore a quiet residential neighborhood. Near Bab el Kasbah, you can climb onto the ramparts for a view over the city. In the evening, residents stroll through the park in front of the kasbah.

Mint tea on a café terrace and street performers in the late afternoon: Assarag Square is the heart of Taroudant. Between it and Talmeklat Square, the covered lanes of the craft souk bring together potters, jewelers, coppersmiths (artisans who work with copper), and carpet sellers. Take time to compare before buying, and always negotiate the price.

The smell reaches you before the sight: the Bab Targhount tannery processes hides just outside Taroudant’s ramparts. Around forty tanners prepare sheep, goat, and dromedary camel hides as visitors watch. Nearby shops sell bags, poufs, and sandals made on-site. Hold a mint leaf under your nose if the smell bothers you.

activities.text: Take a horse-drawn carriage ride around Taroudant’s ramparts late in the day, when the sun warms the ocher walls. These 7.5 km of earthen walls date mainly from the 16th century and the Saadian dynasty. They have earned the city its nickname, “Little Marrakech.” Agree on the price before getting in: the hourly rate is negotiable.

Few souvenirs, plenty of life: Taroudant’s Amazigh souk, the municipal market, mainly sells spices, dried fruit, and household goods. In its open-air section, artisans turn old tires and plastic into saddles, watering troughs, and baskets for donkeys. Enter from Assarag Square. Watch without getting in the way, and ask before taking photos.

Around the Dakar 2027: From the Algarve to Marrakech in 22 Days

visits.text: Built from local earth, Tata’s ksour blend into the landscape. These fortified villages of rammed earth recall the city’s past as a caravan crossroads. Tata’s workshops keep basket weaving, carpet weaving in warm colors, and local pottery traditions alive. Wander through them in the morning before temperatures rise: in summer, they can exceed 45 °C.

activities.text: Beneath the Agadir Lhena palm grove, north of Tata, water flows through khettaras, underground channels that bring groundwater to the gardens. A water clock, or clepsydra, is still used to divide irrigation time among the plots: each family receives water for a measured period. To get there, turn left just after the ford, the crossing through the wadi, drive to the end of the village, then continue on foot along the palm grove trail.

Climb to the highest point in the village of Agadir Lhena for a sweeping view of the Tata oasis. Palm groves line the Tata wadi, a tributary of the Drâa, at the foot of Jbel Bani, the long rocky ridge bordering the southern Anti-Atlas. A series of oases stretches from Agadir Lhena to Tiguisselt. Go up in the late afternoon, when the light is softer and the heat has subsided.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: Taza was briefly the Almohad capital in the 12th century, and around 3 km of ramparts from that period still surround its medina, the old town perched on a hill. The finest stretch is near Bab er-Rih, the “Gate of the Wind.” From there, the views reach the Rif on one side and the Middle Atlas on the other. Bring a jacket.

The Great Mosque of Taza, founded by the Almohads in 1135 and expanded in the 13th century, rises above the rooftops near Bab er-Rih. It is closed to non-Muslims and difficult to make out from outside. Just look at the minaret, then follow the main street through the souks. The medina is explored on foot, without a car.

days_plan.itin_title: Around the Dakar 2027: From the Algarve to Marrakech in 22 Days

visits.text: Behind crumbling earthen walls, the kasbah of Télouet hides reception rooms adorned with zellige (mosaics of small glazed tiles), carved stucco (plaster sculpted in relief), and painted cedar ceilings. The Glaoui family began building it around 1860. In 1893, a snowstorm stranded the army of Sultan Hassan I nearby. Madani El Glaoui supplied the court for several weeks and later became grand vizier, the equivalent of a prime minister. Since the 2023 earthquake, only some of the rooms have been open to visitors, with a guide included in the admission ticket.

activities.text: Télouet’s salt mines partly explain the Glaoui family’s wealth. Their kasbah stood on one of the main caravan routes between Marrakech and the southern valleys on the edge of the Sahara. Salt traveled alongside other goods. Near the village, a salt mine is still operating and can be visited. Ask in the village or check with your kasbah guide for directions.

days_plan.itin_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud

places.name: Tétouan

visits.text: Small but complete: that is how UNESCO describes Tetouan’s World Heritage–listed medina. After the Reconquista, the reconquest of Spain by Christian monarchs, refugees expelled from Andalusia rebuilt the city. A wall roughly 5 km long surrounds it, with seven gates. Follow the main streets connecting these gates: they lead to squares, mosques, and artisan quarters. An official guide will save you unnecessary detours.

Smaller and less colorful than those in Fez, Tetouan’s tanneries make no attempt to impress. A tannery is a workshop where animal hides are processed into leather in vats. This one dates to the late 15th or early 16th century. Look for the small door to the left of Bab Mkabar, one of the medina’s gates, and keep a few dirhams handy for a tip.

“The cleanest and best built”: that was explorer Charles de Foucauld’s assessment of Tetouan’s mellah in 1883. A mellah is the former Jewish quarter of a Moroccan city. This one had as many as six thousand Jewish residents in the late 19th century. Look for its houses with second-floor balconies and paired pointed-arch windows, which distinguish it from the rest of the medina.

An old bastion, a defensive structure built around 1830 above the Bab el-Okla gate, houses Tetouan’s ethnographic museum. It reopened in January 2022. Ethnography studies ways of life: here, clothing, jewelry, and instruments tell the story of daily life in the city. One room presents the squndo, a 15th-century water distribution network that served the medina. Finish in the small garden, with views of the city and the Rif Mountains.

Step inside the School of Arts and Crafts, just outside Bab el-Okla. Founded in 1919 under the Spanish protectorate, it trains artisans in Moroccan and Andalusian crafts. Since 1928, it has occupied a richly decorated building surrounded by a garden. Visit Monday through Friday, as the school does not receive visitors on weekends; on Fridays, it takes a long midday break.

If Lixus left you wanting more, Tetouan’s archaeological museum rounds out the visit. It displays mosaics, Latin inscriptions, and amphorae from Lixus and Tamuda, another ancient city in the region. A scale model depicts the M’Zora cromlech, a circle of large standing stones in northern Morocco. The museum is open Wednesday through Monday; allow time for its Arab-Andalusian garden.

The Ensanche, the new town built by the Spanish west of the medina, is a reminder that Tetouan was the capital of the Spanish protectorate from 1913 to 1956. Residents call it Chanti. Its five-story buildings have stores on the ground floor. The Church of Our Lady of Victories, consecrated in 1925, dominates Moulay el-Mehdi Square. Finish on pedestrian-only Mohammed V Avenue, where cafés and used-book sellers bring the street to life in the evening.

Trains no longer stop at Tetouan’s old station, yet people still come through its doors. The Modern Art Center has occupied the building since 2013. It mainly showcases contemporary Moroccan and Andalusian artists, and its temporary exhibitions can be worth a detour. Admission is free. It is open Tuesday through Saturday, with a midday break: come in the morning or late afternoon.

activities.text: Crisp on the outside and fragrant with lemon inside: that is Tetouan-style pastilla. Pastilla is an oven-baked pie made with very thin sheets of dough and a meat filling. In Tetouan, it is prepared with chicken, eggs, and lemon. Order it at a restaurant in the medina and share it with a group, as it is filling.

visits.text: The water is salty, yet palm trees grow all around: the Tissint waterfalls tumble over rocks in the heart of the oasis. You can swim here to cool off; keep your sandals on, as the wet rock is slippery. The village’s name is also familiar to scientists. In July 2011, a meteorite that fell 48 km to the south was identified as a piece of the planet Mars, thanks to gases from the Martian atmosphere trapped inside the rock.

Disguised as a Jewish traveler, French explorer Charles de Foucauld stayed in Tissint while exploring Morocco. His account, Reconnaissance au Maroc, published in 1888, earned him the gold medal of the Société de géographie. A village guide can take you to his poorly maintained house, about 400 m downstream from the spring. The route passes through the old village’s covered alleys, sheltered from the sun.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Morocco in 10 Days: Erg Chigaga and Tafraoute

visits.text: Tizi n’Tichka Pass was long listed at 2,260 m, but a GPS measurement taken in 2022 puts it at about 2,205 m. It remains the highest of North Africa’s major road passes. The French army laid out the road in the 1930s along an old caravan trail. Its name means “pass of the pastures” in Tamazight, the Berber language. On a clear day, the view stretches as far as Toubkal. From December to March, snow can close the road: check the weather before setting out.

activities.text: Stop in Taddert, a village beside the N9, roughly halfway between Marrakech and Ouarzazate. Travelers stop here for a bite to eat or to browse local crafts before tackling Tizi n’Tichka Pass. The road has been modernized and is much safer than it once was. The curves and trucks still demand attention: take a break here if you have been driving since morning.

days_plan.itin_title: High Atlas in 7 Days: Ourika, Imlil, Télouet, and Ouzoud

visits.text: End the weekend on the hill of the Marinid Tombs, an eight-minute walk from Borj Nord. The entire medina of Fez stretches out before you, with its tightly packed houses and minarets. This 14th-century necropolis is attributed to the Marinids, the dynasty that built the Bou Inania and Al-Attarine madrasas. Two tall, ruined mausoleums with large horseshoe arches remain. Access is free, with no facilities: bring water. Come with others and take a petit taxi back down before nightfall, as thefts have been reported here in the evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Fez in 2 days: medina, madrasas, tannery, and Mellah

visits.text: If you arrive at the Saadian Tombs when they open, around 9 a.m., you will have a shorter wait to see the Hall of the Twelve Columns. This royal necropolis was built primarily by Sultan Ahmed al-Mansour, who died in 1603. His tomb lies in this hall, beneath twelve columns of Carrara marble, a white marble from Italy. Later, Sultan Moulay Ismaïl walled up most of the entrances. The French historic monuments service rediscovered the site in 1917, then opened it to the public. The rooms are viewed from behind barriers. Admission is 100 dirhams, payable in cash.

days_plan.itin_title: Marrakech in 3 Days: Medina, Palaces, Souks, and Gardens

visits.text: Five watchtowers, attributed to the Portuguese by the Moroccan National Tourist Office, gave the village of Torres de Alcala its name. Torres means “towers” in Spanish. You are in Al Hoceima National Park, established in 2004, which protects 50 km of coastline and part of the sea. Climb up to the ruins for a view of the bay, then head down to the pebble-and-sand beach at the mouth of the Beni Boufrah River.

A rocky islet 500 m offshore encloses the bay of Cala Iris, a few kilometers to the west. The small port shelters around thirty fishing boats. The islet is part of the national park: it is one of the few places where the ferruginous limpet, an endangered shellfish that clings to rocks, survives. Do not collect anything from the rocks, and swim at the beach of sand mixed with pebbles.

activities.text: If you still have energy, follow the coastal trail east from Cala Iris. Reaching the area around Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera requires a long hike: allow enough time for the round trip. This rock has belonged to Spain since 1564. In 1930, an earthquake connected it to the coast with an 85 m sandbar. Directly opposite stood Badis, the port that served the inland city of Fez from the 14th to the 16th century. If you do not have enough time for the round trip, walk along the trail for 30 minutes to enjoy the coastal views, then retrace your steps.

visits.text: A paradise that depends on rain: in summer, the river in Paradise Valley runs low and the greenery fades. This valley along the Tamraght River (locally, rivers are called oueds), in the foothills of the High Atlas, is lined with palm trees and clear pools where you can swim. From the parking lot, an easy trail reaches the pools in about 30 minutes. Ideally, visit in late winter or early spring, when the river is full.

activities.text: You can extend your Paradise Valley walk by following trails that climb above the cliffs along the Tamraght River. Wear shoes with ankle support and bring plenty of water. Avoid jumping from rocks into the pools when the water is low: accidents have happened here. To continue to Imouzzer des Ida Outanane, plan a round-trip drive from Paradise Valley, followed by a walk to the waterfalls. In this village perched at 1,250 m, the falls flow mainly from January to March.

visits.text: The mosaics alone are worth the detour: in Volubilis, a Roman city inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1997, they remain in their original places inside the houses. Look for the mosaic of the Labors of Hercules, then follow the main street up to the Arch of Caracalla, which dates from 217. The site opens around 8:30 a.m. There is almost no shade, so bring water.

From the ruins, you will spot a small white town on a hillside: Moulay Idriss Zerhoun, about 5 km away. It is home to the tomb of Idris I, founder of the Idrisid dynasty, and a pilgrimage takes place there every year. Climb to the upper part of town for the view. A short stop is enough on the way to Fez.

visits.text: “Timbuktu 52 days”: Zagora’s famous sign showed how long it took to reach this city in Mali across the Sahara, on foot or by dromedary camel. The original has been replaced by a mural, but the old sign still exists. Stop for a photo as you enter town: it is the most evocative reminder of the caravan era.

Amezrou Kasbah is worth a detour precisely because people still live there. In Zagora’s palm grove, you enter through a maze of narrow streets where families live. The path leading there follows a canal shaded by palm trees. Be discreet and do not photograph residents without their permission.

activities.text: Hike up Jbel Zagora, the mountain overlooking the city, on a 3.8 km loop. Allow nearly two hours for about 250 m of elevation gain over rocky terrain, with white arrows marking the way in places. At the foot of the mountain stand the remains of a fortress built by the Almoravids, a medieval Berber dynasty. Set out early and bring water: from the summit, at 966 m, the view takes in Zagora and the Drâa palm grove.

visits.text: If you see passersby ducking under a beam across the alley, you are approaching the Moulay Idriss II zawiya. A zawiya is a shrine built around a saint’s tomb. These beams mark the boundary of the holy site: until 1912, non-Muslims and pack animals were not allowed to pass beyond them. The tomb belongs to Idriss II, who ruled from 807 to 828 and is traditionally considered the founder of Fez. The interior is reserved for Muslims: approach the doors without photographing worshippers.
